1:
Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all explain the eighth day alike, and Ellicott puts it most neatly: as newly-born children remain seven days unclean and enter the covenant privileges of the congregation on the eighth, so the newly-created priests, after a purging of seven days, began their sacred duties on that symbolical day. Clarke supports it from Ainsworth with parallels — circumcision, young beasts, those unclean by leprosy — all imperfect for seven days and perfected on the eighth. Gill weighs the Jewish datings and settles with Aben Ezra for Nisan the eighth. Ellicott adds a point about the company: the elders summoned here are the same representatives who attested the consecration, now called to witness the priests entering on their active duties. Henry finds the timing instructive. The priests had not one day's respite to receive the compliments of their friends, but were employed the very next day — a sign they were not ordained to be idle. He that desires the office of a bishop desires a good work, which must be looked at more than the honour and the benefit; God's spiritual priests have constant work cut out for them, and their consecration was the filling of their hands.

The calf appointed for Aaron's sin offering draws one explanation from four commentators, and only two add to it. Henry reports the Jewish writers' suggestion that a calf was chosen to remind Aaron of his sin in making the golden calf, by which he had rendered himself for ever unworthy of the priesthood, and on which he had reason to reflect with sorrow in all his atonements; Wesley repeats him almost word for word. Clarke observes that no formal atonement for that transgression had yet been made, which is why the explanation is probable. Ellicott makes it evidential: this is the only instance in which a calf is appointed for a sin offering, the offerer commanded to bring it is Aaron, and the reading is so old that the ancient Chaldee version expresses it. On why Aaron sacrificed for himself first, Ellicott suggests expiation of whatever pride he might have fostered at being so distinguished; Henry presses the pastoral consequence, that those who have care of other souls must look to their own first, since we cannot expect acceptance in prayer for others while unreconciled — a charity that must begin at home, though not end there.

Calvin sets the chapter's architecture out first. The earlier part shows how Aaron, after seven days' initiation, began the work entrusted to him; the second how the sacrifices were approved by a divine miracle, ratifying the priesthood God had instituted. He notices too something easy to pass over — that Moses, never appointed priest by any solemn rite, sanctified the others, so that the authority and efficacy of the outward sign should rest in God alone. On the people's offerings Ellicott identifies the parties precisely: the elders Moses summoned are here called the children of Israel, the representatives acting for the people, which is why the Greek version renders the phrase elders here. Clarke notices a difficulty in the animal named for them, since Leviticus elsewhere requires a young bullock for the congregation's sin and a kid for a ruler's; he suspects it may have been meant for the elders themselves, though he allows the commoner solution, which Wesley also gives, that the earlier law was for a particular sin and this for sin in general. Then the promise. Wesley notes the Hebrew says the Lord hath appeared, speaking of a thing to come as though past, which is frequent in scripture and gives the more assurance; Calvin adds that though Moses seems to address the whole people he speaks especially to Aaron's sons, for whom it was no common aid to faith that their office should be thus sealed by God.
7:
Gill and Ellicott both stop on Aaron's waiting to be told, and Ellicott draws the conclusion. Though now the installed high priest, he did not approach the altar till Moses called him, showing the representatives of the people that he had not taken the honour to himself but had it by the call of God through Moses — which is the apostle's point, that no man takes this honour to himself but he that is called of God, as was Aaron. Keil explains the order, and the explanation governs the rest of the chapter. The sin offering went first, removing the estrangement from a holy God which sin had caused and clearing the hindrances to approach; the burnt offering followed as the expression of the expiated person's complete surrender; the peace offering came last, at once thanksgiving for mercy received and a seal of covenant fellowship in the sacrificial meal.

That the high priest must atone for himself before atoning for anyone else is remarked by Clarke, Calvin and Wesley alike, and Calvin takes it furthest. The apostle justly infers that the legal priesthood was weak and merely typical; for none can be a true peace-maker but one who, relying on his own perfect innocence, presents himself before God to obtain pardon for others, and who, pure from every blemish, requires no expiation for himself. Clarke says the same briefly: it showed the imperfection of the Levitical law. Wesley adds the pastoral edge: first for thyself, otherwise thou art unfit to do it for the people — God teaching us both the deficiency of that priesthood and how needful it is that ministers stand in his favour themselves, if their ministrations are to be acceptable and profitable. Henry watches what Aaron did and finds two things. He slew the victim with his own hands, doing the work of the inferior priests, since great as he was he must think nothing below him that he could do for God's honour; and as Moses had shown him how to do it, so he showed his sons, that being the best way of teaching, and the way parents should instruct their children. Henry notes too that all this was done besides the burnt sacrifice of the morning, whence he draws that our accustomed devotions, morning and evening, alone and in our families, must not be omitted on any pretence — whatever is added, these must not be diminished.

Why the blood never entered the holy place Ellicott, Wesley and Keil all explain alike. Ordinarily the blood of a sin offering for the high priest or the people was taken inside; here Aaron simply put some on the horns of the brazen altar, as Moses had at the consecration, because though high priest he had no access to the sanctuary until this sacrifice qualified him. Wesley states the distinction most sharply: in the earlier law the priest is supposed complete in his office, here he is but entering it, and must sanctify himself at the brazen altar before he can be admitted where the altar of incense stands. What fire consumed them is less settled. Ellicott and Wesley both say ordinary fire, the miraculous fire not issuing until the people's burnt offering was made; Wesley adds that it was lawful, being done at the command of Moses, and that nothing is expressly said to be consumed by the heavenly fire except the burnt offering with its fat. Henry canvasses three views — ordinary fire, the pieces laid ready for fire from heaven, or Bishop Patrick's compromise that Aaron burnt his own with common fire and laid the people's ready — then offers his own: that the fire from the Lord fastened on what was there, put out the fire Aaron had kindled, as a greater fire puts out a less, and suddenly consumed what the lesser would have consumed slowly.
14:
Ellicott follows the ritual detail by detail; two of his notes stand out. On the washing and burning he observes that no special fire was to be kindled for the burnt offering: it was laid on top of the sin offering already burning. On the turn to the people's sacrifices he marks the transition exactly — being reconciled to God by the atoning sacrifice he had offered for his own share in the sin, Aaron was now qualified to offer the sin offering of the people, and conducted its ritual just as he had conducted his own; whereupon he burnt the flesh outside the camp, for which, Ellicott notes, Moses afterwards reproved him. Keil summarises the remaining stages, the burnt offering presented in the prescribed manner, the meat offering, the peace offerings of bullock and ram with the blood sprinkled round about, and the breasts and right shoulder waved before the Lord. Gill explains what the peace offerings were for: that the people might feast and be glad that atonement had been made for their sins, and their gifts accepted of God.

That all this was done besides the burnt sacrifice of the morning is remarked by Ellicott and Wesley both, and Wesley states the principle in a line — God will not have his ordinary and stated service swallowed up by the extraordinary. Ellicott gives the practical shape of it: Aaron began his priestly functions by first offering the daily morning sacrifice, which took precedence of all others and was never superseded by additional ones. Then the blessing, which every commentator here handles and none treats as a formality. Gill sets down the rabbinic prescriptions for the posture in some detail — the hands raised to the shoulders in the provinces and above the head in the sanctuary, the fingers parted so as to leave five spaces, the palms turned toward the earth. Ellicott reports the same practice as a living one: the descendants of Aaron pronounce this benediction upon the congregation in the synagogue to this day, obliged, in accordance with the words here, to turn their faces to the people, and joining thumbs and forefingers so as to produce a triple division of the hand.

What the gesture meant Calvin states most fully. It was a kind of application of the sacrifice, so that the people might know God was reconciled to them through the priest as their mediator and surety; and when by lifting up their hands the priests testified of God's fatherly favour, their commission was ratified and made efficacious. Calvin finds a memorable instance in the chronicler, where the priests and Levites blessed the people and their prayer came up to God's holy dwelling place, even unto heaven. The fulfilment of the type he sees in Christ, who is not only the source and cause of blessing but publishes it by the gospel with effect, coming to preach peace to them that were afar off and to them that were nigh; and though he no longer speaks in visible form, we know what he says — that whatsoever his disciples bind on earth shall be bound in heaven. Wesley reads the posture the same way, that by it Aaron signified both whence he expected the blessing and his hearty desire of it for the people, and insists that blessing was an act of his priestly office no less than sacrificing. Clarke supplies the form from Numbers and states the purpose of the whole day's work: the sacrifices were made not to confer any obligation on God, but to make atonement for sin and to engage him to dwell among his worshippers and influence them. On the coming down Ellicott and Wesley agree that the altar stood higher than the court, Ellicott adding that the standing-place beside it was reached by a gently sloping dam of earth, since steps were not allowed.
23:
Why the two men went into the tent is not stated, and every commentator here supplies a reason. Gill and Ellicott give the same one, and Ellicott gives it most fully: the sacrifices being ended, there still remained the burning of incense on the golden altar within, so Aaron, conducted by Moses, left the court where the altar of burnt offering stood and went into the holy place; and Moses, having already delivered to him the charge of everything connected with the sacrifices in the court, now committed to him the care of the things within the sanctuary as well, showing him how to offer the incense, how to arrange the shewbread, how to light and trim the lamps. Gill adds Jarchi's word that Moses went in to teach him the business of the incense, and the Targum's, that he went in to pray for the people and for the appearance that had been promised them. Keil dissents from both halves. Not to offer incense, he says, which would undoubtedly have been mentioned; nor yet for the special purpose of praying for the manifestation of the glory. Moses went in to introduce Aaron into the sanctuary in which he was henceforth to serve the Lord, and to present him to the Lord; though there can be no doubt, he grants, that they prayed there for the right discharge of the office entrusted to them.

On coming out they united in bestowing upon the people the blessing they had solicited for them within. Calvin notices the change of subject: what was said of Aaron alone in the previous verse is now ascribed to Moses also, and for a different reason, since though Moses was God's prophet, Aaron in right of his office was the only mediator. Ellicott preserves the words that tradition gives them, from the Chaldee version of the Pentateuch — may the word of the Lord accept your sacrifice with favour, and remit and pardon your sins. Wesley defines the verb: to bless is to pray to God for his blessing upon them, and here particularly for his gracious acceptance of these and all succeeding sacrifices, and for his signification of it by some extraordinary token. Which is what followed. Henry draws the inference the whole day has been building toward — the glory appeared not while the sacrifices were in offering but when the priests prayed, and it was when Moses and Aaron concurred in praying that the people had what they had been waiting for.

God's manifestations of himself, of his glory and grace, Henry says, are commonly given in answer to prayer; when Christ was praying the heavens were opened. What the appearance was neither he nor anyone else will say — no doubt it carried its own evidence along with it — but Ellicott and Wesley both take it for the cloudy pillar shining out: the glory which in a lesser degree always filled the tabernacle now visible in greater effulgence to all the people who witnessed the installation, a miraculous brightness, as Wesley has it, or else a glorious and visible discovery of God's gracious presence and acceptance of the present service. Calvin allows the clause to be read either way, as a statement complete in itself or as running straight on into what follows, in which case the account of the consuming of the sacrifice is its exposition — God appeared when he sent forth the fire. Henry's figure is the one that stays. The glory that had filled the tabernacle now showed itself at the door to those who attended there, as a prince shows himself to the expecting crowd, to gratify them; and those who diligently attend upon God in the way he has appointed shall have such a sight of his glory as shall be abundantly to their satisfaction.
24:
Fire came out from before the Lord, and the commentators are agreed on what that phrase leaves open. Gill and Wesley give the same two possibilities, and Wesley puts it shortest — from the presence of the Lord, that is, from the place where God was in a special manner present, either from heaven or from the holy of holies. What it consumed is the harder question, and Gill canvasses it. Aben Ezra took the burnt offering to mean Aaron's and the people's and the daily oblation together, since the text has said the morning burnt offering was besides these; and the fat, the fat of the calf and ram of Aaron and of the goat and ox and ram of the people, which, though laid on the altar as each was offered, some think were not burnt until now. Bishop Patrick conjectured otherwise — that the presentation of all these victims had taken up the whole day, from the morning oblation until dusk, that the burnt offering consumed here was that of the evening, and that all the rest had been burnt with common fire and this alone with fire from the Lord. Ellicott catches what made the sight unmistakable: the victims that ordinarily continued smouldering on the altar all the day and all the night were consumed suddenly, before the people, by flashes sent out from the luminous cloud.

What was kindled that day was not meant to go out. Wesley notes that the fire now given was to be carefully kept and never suffered to lapse, and was therefore carried in a peculiar vessel on their journeys through the wilderness; Ellicott reports the tradition that the flame which thus issued from the immediate presence of God continued to be nourished on the altar with fuel especially provided by the congregation, and so constituted the perpetual fire. Clarke follows it further down the history — this celestial fire was carefully preserved among the Israelites till the time of Solomon, when it was renewed, and continued among them until the Babylonish captivity. Nor was this the only time God answered in this way. Ellicott lists the later occasions on which he testified his acceptance by the same token: Gideon's offering, Elijah's on Carmel, and Solomon's at the dedication of the Temple.

The people's response Clarke breaks into three. The miracle was done in such a way as gave them the fullest conviction of its reality; they exulted in the thought that the God of almighty power had taken up his abode among them; and they prostrated themselves, intimating the deep sense they had of his goodness, of their own unworthiness, and of the obligation they were under to live in obedience to his will. Ellicott hears in the shout the same words the chronicler records at the dedication, when the sons of Israel saw how the fire came down and the glory of the Lord shone upon the house, and bowed themselves with their faces to the ground and praised him, for he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever. Clarke and Wesley both read the fire forward to Pentecost, and Wesley states it in a sentence: thus the Spirit descended in fire upon the apostles, so ratifying their commission as this ratified that of the priests, and the descent of this holy fire into our souls, to kindle in them devout affections and such a holy zeal as burns up all unholiness, is a certain token of God's gracious acceptance. Clarke adds the condition. As no victim was acceptable that had not been seasoned by this flame, so no soul can present an acceptable oblation but through the influences of the Divine Spirit; and if we hope to see him as he is, we must resemble him.
